description_full: Edison International, through its subsidiaries, engages in the generation and distribution of electric power. The company supplies and delivers through its electrical infrastructure to an approximately 50,000 square-mile area of southern, central, and coastal California. It serves residential, commercial, industrial, public authorities, agricultural, street lighting, and other sectors. The company's distribution network consists of approximately 13,000 circuit-miles of lines ranging from 55 kV to 500 kV and approximately 80 transmission substations; and approximately 38,000 circuit-miles of overhead lines, approximately 32,000 circuit-miles of underground lines, and approximately 730 distribution substations. Edison International was founded in 1886 and is based in Rosemead, California.
ceo_bio: Dr. Pedro J. Pizarro Ph.D. | President, CEO & Director | Age 59 | Compensation: $4.8M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 13K people. Revenue per employee of $1.4M ranks in the top quartile among Utilities peers. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (8/10).
financial_summary: Edison International is a large-cap utilities business with a $22.8B market cap on $19.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The company is burning through $715M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.9× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.6×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (0.8) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Piotroski score 4/9 — below the median for a healthy business
Above-average short interest at 6.4% of float
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Regulatory rate-case risk and rising cost of capital — the allowed return is set by commissions, and the business lives or dies by that negotiation.
Grid modernisation capex burden — aging infrastructure requires massive reinvestment that regulators may not fully allow into rate base, compressing earned returns.
Wildfire and climate liability — extreme weather events create catastrophic, uninsurable losses that can push even investment-grade utilities toward restructuring.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 16% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Trading at a 32% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Valued at a 33% discount to sector median EV/EBITDA
22 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Utilities sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter
Utilities tends to hold up well as investors rotate into defensive names

sect: Its 37% operating margin runs 16pp above the Utilities median (21%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.92x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 2.3% of sector revenue and 4.4% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+28.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 97 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 27% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 0.58, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.57 vs 5y 0.48), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $244.2M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 43% in the 2020 crash, 23% in the 2022 bear market and 56% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 32% below its blended-model fair value of $87.88, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 89%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Utilities peers: P/E 6.3 vs 20.4 and EV/EBITDA 8.4 vs 12.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 70% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of -3.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 10.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $63.03 on average, 6% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 5.6%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.54).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.30x.
ROE of 25% is amplified by 5.3x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 23pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.9x net debt to EBITDA ($158.0M of cash against $40.4B of debt), with interest covered 4.6x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.76 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The current ratio of 0.73 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.9% over 3 years, 7.3% over 5 years and 5.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 31% of profits supports about 1.6% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Capex runs 2.0x depreciation (33.7% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 3, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 97%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $654K sold).
It returns 5.7% a year to shareholders (0.1% in buybacks and 5.9% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 22 consecutive years, raising it 6.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 13,725 employees, each generates about $1.4M of revenue, 1.4x the Utilities median, and productivity has risen 2.8% a year.
Free cash flow is negative, at -$52K per employee.
CEO pay is $4.8M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
